newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia seen dropping changes to mining rules.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia seen dropping changes to mining rules.

text.p: Indonesia's mines and energy ministry is expected to withdraw changes it has proposed to mining regulations in the wake of stiff criticism by foreign mining companies, industry sources said on Friday.
They said mining companies had been summoned to a meeting with the director-general of mining, Adjat Sudradjat, later on Friday to discuss the proposed changes.

A ministry official confirmed the meeting but declined to give details except to say it was over the seventh-generation contracts of work (COW) governing mineral mining and the third-generation contracts of work for the coal sector.

"I have been unofficially informed that the mines and energy ministry will not go ahead with the proposed changes," one industry official told Reuters. He declined to say if his information came from government officials.
"The message I got is the COW will be processed soon without change," he said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "The government is to send the original COW for parliamentary approval soon."
Another industry source said he had also heard of the government move to withdraw the proposals.
He said he had received an letter from Adjat informing him of a meeting later on Friday to discuss the COW.
"I have been hearing that (withdrawal), too, and this (meeting) might be the official notification," he said.

Mining companies were given until last Tuesday to respond to the proposed changes, which include requiring mining companies to allocate at least a 10-percent stake in future ventures to the government for free.

They also covered government proposals that mining companies with operations in Indonesia share capital gains made on stock exchanges outside the country with their shareholders and that the raising of additional capital through a public offering of shares would have to be done in Indonesia.
Some mining analysts said the capital gains proposal would be virtually un-enforceable, while Indonesia did not have the capital to finance large-scale exploration work.
Coal mining companies were, among others, required to divest 51 percent of their equity in future projects to Indonesians by the 10th year of operations.
Adjat said on Tuesday mining companies had submitted their response to the changes but did not give details. He said the proposals were not final and were open to negotiations.
